prompt:
If $G$ is a finite group, we define $\mathrm{soc}(G)$ to be the subgroup generated by all the minimal normal subgroups of $G$.

(a) If $\langle1\rangle\neq N\trianglelefteq G$, show that $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(G)\neq\langle1\rangle$.

(b) Prove that $\mathrm{soc}(\mathrm{soc}(G))=\mathrm{soc}(G)$.

(c) If $\mathrm{soc}(G)=G$, show that every minimal normal subgroup of $G$ is simple.
answer: (a) $N$ contains a minimal normal subgroup of $G$. (b) $S=\mathrm{soc}(G)$ is characteristic, so $\mathrm{soc}(S)\trianglelefteq G$; each minimal normal $N$ of $G$ meets $\mathrm{soc}(S)$ nontrivially by (a) applied in $S$, so $N\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(S)$. (c) For $1\ne H\trianglelefteq M$ ($M$ minimal normal), every other minimal normal $N$ centralizes $M$, so $N_G(H)\supseteq\langle\text{all minimal normals}\rangle=G$ and $H=M$.

solutions.title: Minimal normal subgroups
solutions.body:
**(a)** $G$ is finite and $N\ne1$, so among the nontrivial normal subgroups of $G$ contained in $N$ there is a minimal one, $M$; it is a minimal normal subgroup of $G$, so $M\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(G)$ and $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(G)\supseteq M\ne1$.

**(b)** Let $S=\mathrm{soc}(G)$. Clearly $\mathrm{soc}(S)\subseteq S$. Automorphisms of $G$ permute the minimal normal subgroups of $G$, so $S$ is characteristic in $G$; similarly $\mathrm{soc}(S)$ is characteristic in $S$, hence normal in $G$. Let $N$ be a minimal normal subgroup of $G$. Then $1\ne N\subseteq S$ and $N\trianglelefteq S$, so by (a) applied to the group $S$, $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(S)\ne1$. But $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(S)\trianglelefteq G$ and $N$ is minimal normal in $G$, so $N\cap\mathrm{soc}(S)=N$, i.e. $N\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(S)$. Since $S$ is generated by such $N$, $S\subseteq\mathrm{soc}(S)$. Hence equality.

**(c)** Let $G=\mathrm{soc}(G)$, $M$ a minimal normal subgroup, and $1\ne H\trianglelefteq M$. Let $N$ be any minimal normal subgroup of $G$.
- If $N\ne M$, then $M\cap N$ is normal in $G$ and properly contained in $M$ or $N$, so $M\cap N=1$; hence $[M,N]\subseteq M\cap N=1$, $N$ centralizes $M\supseteq H$, so $N$ normalizes $H$.
- If $N=M$, then $N$ normalizes $H$ because $H\trianglelefteq M$.

Thus $N_G(H)$ contains every minimal normal subgroup, so $N_G(H)\supseteq\mathrm{soc}(G)=G$ and $H\trianglelefteq G$. By minimality of $M$, $H=M$. So $M$ has no normal subgroups other than $1$ and $M$, i.e. $M$ is simple. ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field and suppose $f(x)\in F[x]$ is an irreducible polynomial. Fix an integer $n$ and let $g(x)=f(x^n)$.

(a) If $h(x)$ is any irreducible factor of $g(x)$ in $F[x]$, show that the degree of $h(x)$ is a multiple of the degree of $f(x)$.

(b) Now suppose that $F$ has characteristic $0$ and that it contains a primitive $n$th root of unity. Show that all irreducible factors of $g(x)$ in $F[x]$ have equal degrees.
answer: (a) For a root $\alpha$ of $h$, $\alpha^n$ is a root of $f$, so $\deg h=|F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)|\cdot\deg f$. (b) For roots $\alpha,\beta$ of two factors, an $F$-isomorphism $F(\alpha^n)\to F(\beta^n)$ extends to an automorphism $\tau$ of the splitting field $E$ of $g$; $\tau(\alpha)=\varepsilon\beta$ with $\varepsilon\in F$, so $F(\alpha)\cong F(\beta)$ and the degrees agree.

solutions.title: Tower of degrees and extending isomorphisms
solutions.body:
Work inside an algebraic closure of $F$; take $n\ge1$.

**(a)** Let $\alpha$ be a root of $h$. Since $h$ is irreducible, $\deg h=|F(\alpha):F|$. As $h\mid g$, $f(\alpha^n)=g(\alpha)=0$, and $f$ is irreducible, so $\deg f=|F(\alpha^n):F|$. Since $F\subseteq F(\alpha^n)\subseteq F(\alpha)$,
$$\deg h=|F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)|\cdot|F(\alpha^n):F|=|F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)|\cdot\deg f.$$

**(b)** Let $E$ be a splitting field of $g$ over $F$, and let $h,k$ be irreducible factors of $g$ with roots $\alpha,\beta\in E$. Then $\alpha^n,\beta^n$ are roots of the irreducible $f$, so there is an $F$-isomorphism $\sigma\colon F(\alpha^n)\to F(\beta^n)$ with $\sigma(\alpha^n)=\beta^n$. $E$ is a splitting field of $g$ over $F(\alpha^n)$ and over $F(\beta^n)$, and $\sigma$ fixes the coefficients of $g\in F[x]$. By uniqueness of splitting fields, $\sigma$ extends to an isomorphism $\tau\colon E\to E$ fixing $F$.

Now $\tau(\alpha)^n=\tau(\alpha^n)=\beta^n$, so $\tau(\alpha)=\varepsilon\beta$ for some $n$th root of unity $\varepsilon$ (all $n$th roots of $\beta^n$ are $\zeta^i\beta$ where $\zeta\in F$ is the given primitive root; if $\beta=0$ then $\tau(\alpha)=0$). So $\varepsilon\in F$ and $F(\tau(\alpha))=F(\varepsilon\beta)=F(\beta)$. Since $\tau$ restricts to an $F$-isomorphism $F(\alpha)\to F(\tau(\alpha))=F(\beta)$,
$$\deg h=|F(\alpha):F|=|F(\beta):F|=\deg k.$$ ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over the field $K$ and let $(\ ,\ )\colon V\times V\to K$ be a symmetric bilinear form. For any subspace $U$ of $V$, we let $U^\perp=\{v\in V\mid(U,v)=0\}$. Thus $U^\perp$ is also a subspace of $V$, and the form is nonsingular precisely when $V^\perp=0$.

(a) Show that $\dim U+\dim U^\perp\ge\dim V$ for any subspace $U$ of $V$.

(b) If the form is nonsingular and if $V=U+X$ is the sum of subspaces $U$ and $X$, prove that $\dim U^\perp+\dim X^\perp\le\dim V$.

(c) If the form is nonsingular, show that $\dim U+\dim U^\perp=\dim V$ for any subspace $U$ of $V$.
answer: (a) $U^\perp$ is the kernel of $v\mapsto((u_i,v))_i\in K^r$. (b) $U^\perp\cap X^\perp=(U+X)^\perp=V^\perp=0$. (c) With $X$ a complement of $U$: $\dim U^\perp\le\dim V-\dim X^\perp\le\dim X$ by (b) and (a), so $\dim U+\dim U^\perp\le\dim V$; combine with (a).

solutions.title: Rank–nullity
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $u_1,\dots,u_r$ be a basis of $U$ and define $T\colon V\to K^r$, $T(v)=((u_1,v),\dots,(u_r,v))$. $T$ is linear and $\ker T=U^\perp$ (a vector orthogonal to a basis of $U$ is orthogonal to $U$). By rank–nullity, $\dim V=\dim\operatorname{im}T+\dim U^\perp\le r+\dim U^\perp$.

**(b)** A vector in $U^\perp\cap X^\perp$ is orthogonal to $U+X=V$, so $U^\perp\cap X^\perp=V^\perp=0$. Hence $U^\perp+X^\perp$ is direct and $\dim U^\perp+\dim X^\perp=\dim(U^\perp\oplus X^\perp)\le\dim V$.

**(c)** Choose a complement $X$ with $V=U\oplus X$. By (b) and (a) (applied to $X$),
$$\dim U^\perp+\dim X^\perp\le\dim V\le\dim X+\dim X^\perp,$$
so $\dim U^\perp\le\dim X$. Thus $\dim U+\dim U^\perp\le\dim U+\dim X=\dim V$, and (a) gives the reverse inequality. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be a (not necessarily finite) abelian group and let $B$ be a subgroup of $A$.

(a) If $B$ is a direct factor of $A$, show that $B$ is a direct factor of every subgroup $C$ satisfying $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$.

(b) Conversely, assume that $B$ is a direct factor of every subgroup $C$ such that $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$ and $C/B$ is cyclic. If $|A:B|<\infty$, show that $B$ is a direct factor of $A$.
answer: (a) If $A=B\oplus X$, the modular law gives $C=B\oplus(X\cap C)$. (b) Write the finite group $A/B=\bigoplus\bar C_i$ with $\bar C_i$ cyclic, split $C_i=B\oplus X_i$, and check $A=B\oplus(X_1+\cdots+X_n)$.

solutions.title: Modular law and cyclic decomposition
solutions.body:
Write $A$ additively.

**(a)** Let $A=B\oplus X$ and $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$. By the modular law (valid since $B\subseteq C$), $C=(B+X)\cap C=B+(X\cap C)$, and $B\cap(X\cap C)\subseteq B\cap X=0$. So $C=B\oplus(X\cap C)$.

**(b)** $\bar A=A/B$ is a finite abelian group, so $\bar A=\bar C_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\bar C_n$ with each $\bar C_i$ cyclic. Let $C_i\supseteq B$ be the preimage of $\bar C_i$. By hypothesis $C_i=B\oplus X_i$ for some subgroup $X_i$. Put $X=X_1+\cdots+X_n$.

- $A=B+X$: since $\bar A=\sum\bar C_i$, $A=C_1+\cdots+C_n=\sum(B+X_i)=B+X$.
- $B\cap X=0$: if $a=x_1+\cdots+x_n\in B$ with $x_i\in X_i$, then $0=\bar a=\bar x_1+\cdots+\bar x_n$ with $\bar x_i\in\bar C_i$; as the sum of the $\bar C_i$ is direct, each $\bar x_i=0$, i.e. $x_i\in B\cap X_i=0$. So $a=0$.

Hence $A=B\oplus X$. ∎
